title: Jeremiah 48:18–28
context: The oracle continues with calls to the towns of Moab to come down, watch, and wail as judgment falls on the plain country. A list of cities follows, many of uncertain location. The LORD declares that Moab’s horn is cut off and commands that Moab be made drunk because he magnified himself against the LORD and mocked Israel. The cup imagery recalls Jeremiah 25:15-21, where Moab is among the nations made to drink. The section ends with a call to flee to the rocks like a dove.

verses.text: “You daughter who dwells in Dibon, come down from your glory, and sit in thirst; for the destroyer of Moab has come up against you. He has destroyed your strongholds.
verses.arminianNotes: You daughter who dwells in Dibon, come down from your glory, and sit in thirst; Arminian readers see a city personified and brought low, called to exchange honor for humiliation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Dibon is often identified with a site north of the Arnon, though identifications should be held loosely. An inscription often cited in Moabite history is associated with that area.

verses.text: Inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way and watch. Ask him who flees, and her who escapes; say, ‘What has been done?’
verses.arminianNotes: Inhabitant of Aroer, stand by the way and watch. Arminian readers picture people at the roadside asking those who flee for news, a vivid image of a land in confusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the question, What has been done? Aroer is commonly placed near the Arnon gorge, though, as with other sites in the chapter, the identification is tentative.

verses.text: Moab is disappointed; for it is broken down. Wail and cry! Tell it by the Arnon, that Moab is laid waste.
verses.arminianNotes: Moab is disappointed; for it is broken down. Arminian readers hear the call to wail and cry and to tell it by the Arnon, so that the news spreads along the land’s main river.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Arnon was a traditional border of Moab (Numbers 21:13). The announcement at the river makes the fall known throughout the region.

verses.text: Judgment has come on the plain country— on Holon, on Jahzah, on Mephaath,
verses.arminianNotes: Judgment has come on the plain country— Arminian readers see the list of towns as a way of showing that no part of Moab escapes, from the larger cities to lesser places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath are not securely identified. The list itself, rather than precise geography, conveys the reach of the judgment.

verses.text: on Dibon, on Nebo, on Beth Diblathaim,
verses.arminianNotes: on Dibon, on Nebo, on Beth Diblathaim, Arminian readers note that names already mentioned in the oracle return, so that the list gathers up the towns into one sweep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Beth Diblathaim is otherwise little known, and its location is uncertain. The repeated names of Dibon and Nebo tie this list to the opening of the chapter.

verses.text: on Kiriathaim, on Beth Gamul, on Beth Meon,
verses.arminianNotes: on Kiriathaim, on Beth Gamul, on Beth Meon, Arminian readers see the list continuing in a steady rhythm, each name a community whose life will be disrupted by the coming judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Beth Gamul and Beth Meon are identified only tentatively. Kiriathaim appears again after 48:1, and Ezekiel 25:9 also names it among Moab’s towns.

verses.text: on Kerioth, on Bozrah, and on all the cities of the land of Moab, far or near.
verses.arminianNotes: on Kerioth, on Bozrah, and on all the cities of the land of Moab, far or near. Arminian readers see the list closing with a sweeping phrase that includes every city of the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Kerioth also appears in Amos 2:2, which speaks of the palaces of Kerioth. This Bozrah is usually distinguished from the Edomite Bozrah of 49:22, though that is debated.

verses.text: The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The horn of Moab is cut off, and his arm is broken, Arminian readers see power stripped away, since horn and arm are common images of strength in Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the LORD himself pronounces the end of Moab’s strength. The images summarize the preceding list in two short lines of loss.

verses.text: “Make him drunk, for he magnified himself against the LORD. Moab will wallow in his vomit, and he also will be in derision.
verses.arminianNotes: Make him drunk, for he magnified himself against the LORD. Arminian readers see the cup of judgment from Jeremiah 25:15-21, where Moab is listed among the nations, and read the image soberly as humiliation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the cause is stated plainly: Moab magnified himself against the LORD, a charge also made in Zephaniah 2:8-10. The image of disgrace answers Moab’s pride rather than describing a literal scene.

verses.text: For wasn’t Israel a derision to you? Was he found among thieves? For as often as you speak of him, you shake your head.
verses.arminianNotes: For wasn’t Israel a derision to you? Arminian readers see Moab’s mockery of Israel turned back on itself, as the one who scorned now becomes an object of derision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the question, Was he found among thieves? Moab treated Israel with contempt, shaking its head, and Zephaniah 2:8 also mentions Moab’s reproach against the LORD’s people.

verses.text: You inhabitants of Moab, leave the cities, and dwell in the rock. Be like the dove that makes her nest over the mouth of the abyss.
verses.arminianNotes: You inhabitants of Moab, leave the cities, and dwell in the rock. Arminian readers hear a call to flee from cities to rocky places, as people seek refuge wherever they can.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of the dove that makes her nest over the mouth of the abyss. The picture is of fragile refuge in dangerous places, far from settled life.
